newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine growth strong again, but threats loom.
newsitem.headline: Argentine growth strong again, but threats loom.

text.p: Argentina's economy has sprung back to life after a couple of years' convalescence but its new vigor could still be dulled by a vicious rise in U.S. interest rates or a big Brazilian devaluation, analysts said.
"After (President Carlos) Menem, the most important man for Argentina is (U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman) Alan Greenspan," economist Miguel Broda said recently.
"What happens to interest rates is the biggest international problem Argentina has...it is the biggest doubt hanging over the optimistic Argentine scenario," he said.

Argentina got a bad case of whiplash after Mexico's peso skidded downwards in December 1994, and its economy contracted by 4.6 percent in 1995. Limping back onto the road in 1996, Argentina managed to regain most of its lost ground, with 4.4 percent expansion.
Now firmly back on the highway to growth, analysts are more optimistic than even the government. They say that growth in 1997 should be six percent, beating the official forecast of five percent.
The analysts say bank deposits -- already at levels 35 percent higher than before the Mexican peso tumbled -- should continue chugging higher, and export growth looks set to continue strongly.
The benevolent outlook took on an extra tint of rose last week when ratings agency Standard & Poor's boosted its rating for Argentina's foreign currency debt by one notch.
In the agency's eyes, Argentina is now less risky than Brazil and about the same as Mexico. But it is still two notches more of a gamble than Chile.
World economic growth and healthy commodity prices should also help Argentine prospects.
But happiness is never absolute. For one thing, unemployment is stuck at 17.3 percent. And one of the dark clouds which could roll over the horizon would be more restrictive American monetary policy.

"If short-term rates rise as expected by between 50 and 100 basis points, and this then contaminates long-term rates, then we could see a restriction on long-term financing for the government and for business, and that would affect growth," said Nicolas Dujovne, of Macroeconomica.
"The short-term outlook continues to depend on whether interest rates rise and the behavior of international markets," he added.
Ines Piccinino, economist for Asesores Economicos, also forecast scarcer and dearer financing but made it clear that "we won't go through the 1995 crisis again."

Argentina's woes in 1995 were caused by a liquidity drought. The sudden, sharp shortage of international funds shook Argentina's banking system and once again exposed the country's reliance on external finance due to its low internal savings rate.
Salomon Brothers recently warned that Argentine markets could go through a rough patch if rates rose.

Analysts say Argentina's banking system is in better shape than it was before the Mexican crisis -- dubbed locally "the Tequila Effect," partly due to the creation of a $6 billion banking security insurance program by the Central Bank to deal with any future liquidity crisis.
But the other big potential problem for Argentina is Brazil -- specifically if Brazil took further measures to plug its trade gap by restricting imports or by a big devaluation of its real currency.

"Brazil is an attractive trading partner because it has a big market, but its unpredictability makes it very dangerous. The deficit and the postponement of structural changes mean that its stability is precarious," said economist Marco Rebosov for the private CEAL consultancy.
Another economist, Rudiger Dornbusch, warned that a Brazilian devaluation "could affect Argentina like a mini Tequila Effect."
But he said no devaluation was likely until after Brazil's 1998 elections, in which President Fernando Henrique Cardoso is seeking a second term.
